rationale: A wins because it keeps its knife inside the facts and turns uncertainty into proof requirements instead of decorating it. “Whoop puts a cleared ECG and an uncleared blood-pressure estimate on the same wrist” is a real regulatory story with a clean beat, antagonist, and document trail. B has better headline snap, but “Whoop Finally Has FDA-Cleared ECG. Apple Watch Has Had It for Years.” imports a named competitor and timeline the update did not supply. That is how a pitch gets fact-checked to death before lunch.
gaps_in_A: “uncleared blood-pressure estimate” is likely right, but the update only says non-medical wellness estimate, not diagnostic; the angle needs FDA-status confirmation before using that word in a pitch.
“What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on” overstates the supplied fact. The update says an advisory board reviewed the features; review is not sign-off.
“false positives, worried-well referrals” is plausible clinical context, but not in the update. Keep it as a reporter question unless Whoop has validation or clinician evidence.
gaps_in_B: “Apple Watch Has Had It for Years” invents a named competitor and timeline not provided in the update. The facts only say competitors already ship FDA-cleared ECG.
“a condition linked to stroke and heart failure” brings in an external medical claim. True or not, it is not in the supplied record, and this exercise punishes that.
“The wearable industry has spent years positioning cuffless blood pressure monitoring as the next frontier” is a fake news peg unless you can source it. Right now it is a vibes scaffolding.

“structured it to avoid diagnostic liability” assigns legal intent from wording alone. The safer angle asks whether the wellness framing kept the feature outside FDA review; it does not declare the strategy.
